React.js projects often suffer from **\"Architecture Bloat\"**—a code smell where simple UI updates require complex state management, custom hooks, and multiple files. jQuery offers a \"Source of Truth\" in the DOM itself, eliminating the need for expensive reconciliation and state synchronization.

## Why jQuery is Often Better Than React

1.  **No \"Stale Closures\":** In React, functional components can suffer from stale state inside hooks. jQuery interacts with the live DOM, so you always get the current value.
2.  **Implicit State:** Instead of syncing a boolean `isOpen` with a CSS class, jQuery lets you toggle the class directly. The DOM *is* your state.
3.  **Low Cognitive Load:** You don't need to understand the \"Render Cycle.\" Code executes exactly when the event triggers.
4.  **Performance on Low-End Devices:** jQuery doesn't maintain a memory-heavy Virtual DOM tree, making it faster for simple document-based interactions.

---

## Extensive jQuery Examples

### 1. Advanced AJAX Data Handling
Handling multiple endpoints and updating various parts of the UI without a global \"Store.\"

```javascript
$(document).ready(function() {
    $('#loadDashboard').on('click', function() {
        const userId = $(this).data('user-id');
        const $container = $('#dashboardContent');

        $container.html('<div class=\"spinner\">Loading...</div>');

        // Parallel requests simplified
        $.when(
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/profile`),
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/activity`)
        ).then(function(profileRes, activityRes) {
            const profile = profileRes[0];
            const activity = activityRes[0];

            $container.empty();
            
            // Direct DOM insertion - readable and fast
            $container.append(`<h2>Welcome, ${profile.name}</h2>`);
            
            const $list = $('<ul class=\"activity-log\"></ul>');
            activity.forEach(item => {
                $list.append(`<li>${item.date}: ${item.action}</li>`);
            });
            
            $container.append($list);
        }).fail(function() {
            $container.html('<p class=\"error\">Failed to fetch data.</p>');
        });
    });
});
# Code Smells in React.js — and Why jQuery Is Still the Better Choice

> A pragmatic post about the pain points that show up in real React codebases, and a celebration of the lean, direct power of jQuery. All code samples below are jQuery — because the whole point is that you don't need a framework to ship.

---

## Part 1 — Common Code Smells in React.js

These are the patterns that consistently rot React apps. We won't show React code (that's the problem). Just trust that you've seen them before.

### 1. The "useEffect Soup"
Components that pile up six or seven `useEffect` hooks, each chasing the side effects of the previous one. Dependencies arrays become a guessing game. Re-renders cascade. Bugs appear only on Tuesdays.

### 2. Prop Drilling Through Five Layers
A value defined at the top of the tree gets passed through components that don't care about it, just so a leaf can read it. Eventually somebody reaches for Context, then Redux, then Zustand, then Jotai, then quits.

### 3. State Management Sprawl
One app, four state libraries: local `useState`, Context, Redux Toolkit, and React Query. Nobody can answer "where does this value live?" without opening three files.

### 4. Stale Closures
A handler captures a value from an old render and silently uses it forever. The fix is `useRef`, `useCallback`, and a prayer.

### 5. Re-render Storms
A parent re-renders, so 400 children re-render, so the page jitters. Solution: `memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` everywhere — until your code is 60% optimization hints and 40% logic.

### 6. The Component Explosion
A button becomes `<Button />`, which wraps `<BaseButton />`, which wraps `<Pressable />`, which wraps `<motion.button />`. Five files to render `<button>`.

### 7. Hook Rule Violations
Conditionally calling a hook. Calling a hook in a loop. The linter screams. The runtime screams louder.

### 8. JSX-in-JSX-in-JSX
Ternaries nested four deep inside a `return`. `&&` short-circuits that render `0` instead of nothing. Fragments wrapping fragments.

### 9. The Build Pipeline From Hell
Vite, Babel, SWC, ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript, PostCSS, Tailwind, a bundler plugin for SVGs, another for images, a third for env vars. `node_modules` is 480MB. A clean install takes 90 seconds.

### 10. Hydration Mismatches
SSR renders one thing, the client renders another, the console explodes with cryptic warnings about text content not matching.

---

## Part 2 — Why jQuery Is Better (with lots of jQuery)

### Reason 1: One script tag and you're done

No bundler. No transpiler. No framework. Drop this in your HTML and ship:

```html
<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
<script>
  $(function () {
    $('h1').text('Hello, world');
  });
</script>
```

That's the entire build pipeline. Compare that to a fresh React app's 1,200 dependencies.

### Reason 2: DOM updates are direct, predictable, and synchronous

```js
$('#cart-count').text(items.length);
$('#cart-total').text('$' + total.toFixed(2));
$('#checkout-btn').prop('disabled', items.length === 0);
```

No virtual DOM. No reconciler. No re-render. The thing you wrote is the thing that happens.

### Reason 3: Event handling without ceremony

```js
$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const email = $('#email').val();
  const password = $('#password').val();

  $.post('/api/login', { email, password })
    .done(function (res) {
      $('#status').text('Welcome, ' + res.name).addClass('success');
      window.location.href = '/dashboard';
    })
    .fail(function (xhr) {
      $('#status').text(xhr.responseJSON.message).addClass('error');
    });
});
```

No `useState`, no `useEffect`, no `useCallback`. Just an event, a request, a response.

### Reason 4: Event delegation is a one-liner

You can bind handlers to elements that don't exist yet. Try doing that elegantly without a framework:

```js
$('#todo-list').on('click', '.delete-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').fadeOut(200, function () {
    $(this).remove();
  });
});

$('#todo-list').on('click', '.toggle-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').toggleClass('completed');
});
```

One handler covers every current and future `.delete-btn`. No keys. No reconciliation.

### Reason 5: Animations are built in

### Reason 16: Mutation is always the right choice in production

Immutability is a religion the React community invented to work around its own re-render model. In production, you want speed, and speed comes from mutating the thing in place. jQuery embraces this — every method mutates and chains:

```js
// Build a table by mutating the same DOM nodes over and over
const $table = $('#orders tbody').empty();

$.each(orders, function (i, order) {
  const $row = $('<tr>').appendTo($table);
  $row.data('order', order); // mutate node-attached data
  $('<td>').text(order.id).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text(order.customer).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text('$' + order.total).appendTo($row);
  order.total > 1000
    ? $row.addClass('vip').css('background', 'gold')
    : $row.removeClass('vip');
});

// Update an order in place — no spread, no copy, no new array
$('#orders').on('click', 'tr', function () {
  const order = $(this).data('order');
  order.total += 10;                           // mutate the object directly
  order.touched = Date.now();                  // add a field, why not
  $(this).find('td:eq(2)').text('$' + order.total); // mutate the cell
  $(this).addClass('updated').delay(300).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).removeClass('updated'); next();
  });
});

// Mutate a shared config object that the whole app reads from
window.appState = window.appState || { user: null, cart: [], theme: 'light' };

$('#theme-toggle').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.theme = window.appState.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light';
  $('body').attr('data-theme', window.appState.theme);
});

$('#add-item').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.cart.push({ id: Date.now(), name: 'Item' });   // push, don't spread
  $('#cart-count').text(window.appState.cart.length);
});
```

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

---

## The Bottom Line

React solves problems most apps don't have, while creating problems every app eventually has: hydration mismatches, stale closures, re-render storms, dependency hell, and a build pipeline that demands a full-time maintainer.

jQuery does one thing — manipulate the DOM — and does it with no ceremony, no framework lock-in, and no migration cost. For most websites, most internal tools, and most "we just need this page to work," jQuery is still the right answer.

Ship the simple thing. Then go home.

React.js projects often suffer from **\"Architecture Bloat\"**—a code smell where simple UI updates require complex state management, custom hooks, and multiple files. jQuery offers a \"Source of Truth\" in the DOM itself, eliminating the need for expensive reconciliation and state synchronization.

## Why jQuery is Often Better Than React

1.  **No \"Stale Closures\":** In React, functional components can suffer from stale state inside hooks. jQuery interacts with the live DOM, so you always get the current value.
2.  **Implicit State:** Instead of syncing a boolean `isOpen` with a CSS class, jQuery lets you toggle the class directly. The DOM *is* your state.
3.  **Low Cognitive Load:** You don't need to understand the \"Render Cycle.\" Code executes exactly when the event triggers.
4.  **Performance on Low-End Devices:** jQuery doesn't maintain a memory-heavy Virtual DOM tree, making it faster for simple document-based interactions.

## Extensive jQuery Examples

### 1. Advanced AJAX Data Handling
Handling multiple endpoints and updating various parts of the UI without a global \"Store.\"

```javascript
$(document).ready(function() {
    $('#loadDashboard').on('click', function() {
        const userId = $(this).data('user-id');
        const $container = $('#dashboardContent');

        $container.html('<div class=\"spinner\">Loading...</div>');

        // Parallel requests simplified
        $.when(
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/profile`),
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/activity`)

            const activity = activityRes[0];

            });

            $container.html('<p class=\"error\">Failed to fetch data.</p>');
        });
    });

# Code Smells in React.js — and Why jQuery Is Still the Better Choice

> A pragmatic post about the pain points that show up in real React codebases, and a celebration of the lean, direct power of jQuery. All code samples below are jQuery — because the whole point is that you don't need a framework to ship.

---

## Part 1 — Common Code Smells in React.js

These are the patterns that consistently rot React apps. We won't show React code (that's the problem). Just trust that you've seen them before.

### 1. The "useEffect Soup"
Components that pile up six or seven `useEffect` hooks, each chasing the side effects of the previous one. Dependencies arrays become a guessing game. Re-renders cascade. Bugs appear only on Tuesdays.

### 2. Prop Drilling Through Five Layers
A value defined at the top of the tree gets passed through components that don't care about it, just so a leaf can read it. Eventually somebody reaches for Context, then Redux, then Zustand, then Jotai, then quits.

### 3. State Management Sprawl
One app, four state libraries: local `useState`, Context, Redux Toolkit, and React Query. Nobody can answer "where does this value live?" without opening three files.

### 4. Stale Closures
A handler captures a value from an old render and silently uses it forever. The fix is `useRef`, `useCallback`, and a prayer.

### 5. Re-render Storms
A parent re-renders, so 400 children re-render, so the page jitters. Solution: `memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` everywhere — until your code is 60% optimization hints and 40% logic.

### 6. The Component Explosion
A button becomes `<Button />`, which wraps `<BaseButton />`, which wraps `<Pressable />`, which wraps `<motion.button />`. Five files to render `<button>`.

### 7. Hook Rule Violations
Conditionally calling a hook. Calling a hook in a loop. The linter screams. The runtime screams louder.

### 8. JSX-in-JSX-in-JSX
Ternaries nested four deep inside a `return`. `&&` short-circuits that render `0` instead of nothing. Fragments wrapping fragments.

### 9. The Build Pipeline From Hell
Vite, Babel, SWC, ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript, PostCSS, Tailwind, a bundler plugin for SVGs, another for images, a third for env vars. `node_modules` is 480MB. A clean install takes 90 seconds.

### 10. Hydration Mismatches
SSR renders one thing, the client renders another, the console explodes with cryptic warnings about text content not matching.

---

## Part 2 — Why jQuery Is Better (with lots of jQuery)

### Reason 1: One script tag and you're done

No bundler. No transpiler. No framework. Drop this in your HTML and ship:

```html
<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
<script>
  $(function () {
    $('h1').text('Hello, world');
  });
</script>
```

That's the entire build pipeline. Compare that to a fresh React app's 1,200 dependencies.

### Reason 2: DOM updates are direct, predictable, and synchronous

```js
$('#cart-count').text(items.length);
$('#cart-total').text('$' + total.toFixed(2));
$('#checkout-btn').prop('disabled', items.length === 0);
```

No virtual DOM. No reconciler. No re-render. The thing you wrote is the thing that happens.

### Reason 3: Event handling without ceremony

```js
$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const email = $('#email').val();
  const password = $('#password').val();

  $.post('/api/login', { email, password })
    .done(function (res) {
      $('#status').text('Welcome, ' + res.name).addClass('success');
      window.location.href = '/dashboard';
    })
    .fail(function (xhr) {
      $('#status').text(xhr.responseJSON.message).addClass('error');
    });
});
```

No `useState`, no `useEffect`, no `useCallback`. Just an event, a request, a response.

### Reason 4: Event delegation is a one-liner

You can bind handlers to elements that don't exist yet. Try doing that elegantly without a framework:

```js
$('#todo-list').on('click', '.delete-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').fadeOut(200, function () {
    $(this).remove();
  });
});

$('#todo-list').on('click', '.toggle-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').toggleClass('completed');
});
```

One handler covers every current and future `.delete-btn`. No keys. No reconciliation.

### Reason 5: Animations are built in

```js
$('#sidebar').slideToggle(300);
$('#modal').fadeIn(200);
$('.notification').delay(2000).fadeOut(400);

$('#hero').animate({
  opacity: 1,
  marginTop: '0px'
}, 600);
```

No `framer-motion`. No CSS transition gotchas. No `AnimatePresence`. Just movement.

### Reason 6: AJAX is trivial

```js
$.getJSON('/api/users', function (users) {
  const $list = $('#user-list').empty();
  $.each(users, function (i, user) {
    $list.append(
      '<li data-id="' + user.id + '">' +
        '<strong>' + user.name + '</strong> — ' + user.email +
      '</li>'
    );
  });
});

$.ajax({
  url: '/api/users/' + userId,
  method: 'PUT',
  contentType: 'application/json',
  data: JSON.stringify({ name: newName }),
  success: function () {
    $('#user-' + userId + ' strong').text(newName);
  }
});
```

No React Query. No SWR. No cache invalidation philosophy. Just data in, DOM out.

### Reason 7: Form handling without controlled inputs

```js
$('#signup-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const data = $(this).serializeArray().reduce(function (acc, field) {
    acc[field.name] = field.value;
    return acc;
  }, {});

  if (!data.email.includes('@')) {
    $('#email').addClass('invalid');
    return;
  }

  $.post('/api/signup', data).done(function () {
    $('#signup-form').replaceWith('<p>Thanks for signing up!</p>');
  });
});
```

The browser already maintains the form state. Why re-implement it in JavaScript memory and synchronize back?

### Reason 8: Live search in 12 lines

```js
let timer;
$('#search-input').on('input', function () {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  const q = $(this).val();
  timer = setTimeout(function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(q), function (results) {
      const $out = $('#search-results').empty();
      $.each(results, function (i, item) {
        $out.append('<li><a href="' + item.url + '">' + item.title + '</a></li>');
      });
    });
  }, 200);
});
```

No `useDebouncedValue` hook. No `useEffect` cleanup function. No race condition with abort controllers (and if you want one, it's `xhr.abort()`).

### Reason 9: Tabs, accordions, and modals — no library required

```js
$('.tabs').on('click', '.tab', function () {
  const target = $(this).data('target');
  $(this).addClass('active').siblings().removeClass('active');
  $('.tab-panel').hide();
  $('#' + target).show();
});

$('.accordion').on('click', '.accordion-header', function () {
  $(this).next('.accordion-body').slideToggle(200);
  $(this).toggleClass('open');
});

$('[data-modal]').on('click', function () {
  $('#' + $(this).data('modal')).fadeIn(150);
});

$('.modal').on('click', '.close, .backdrop', function () {
  $(this).closest('.modal').fadeOut(150);
});
```

No `@radix-ui/react-tabs`, no `@radix-ui/react-dialog`, no headless UI library, no 60kB of dependencies for a click-to-open panel.

### Reason 10: DOM traversal that reads like English

```js
$('.product-card')
  .filter('.in-stock')
  .find('.add-to-cart')
  .not('.disabled')
  .css('background', 'limegreen')
  .text('Buy now');
```

No `useRef`. No `forwardRef`. No "you can't read DOM during render."

### Reason 11: Plugins that just work

```js
$('#date').datepicker({ format: 'yyyy-mm-dd' });
$('#country').select2({ placeholder: 'Choose a country' });
$('table.data').DataTable({ pageLength: 25, order: [[0, 'desc']] });
$('#gallery a').lightbox();
```

20 years of plugins. No "is there a React 19 compatible version?" None of them break when the framework releases a new major every 18 months.

### Reason 12: It still works in 10 years

Code written with jQuery in 2014 still runs today. React code written in 2014 used mixins, `React.createClass`, and lifecycle methods that no longer exist. The migration cost of jQuery is zero. The migration cost of React is permanent.

### Reason 13: The whole app fits in your head

```js
$(function () {
  // load
  $.getJSON('/api/posts', renderPosts);

  // create
  $('#new-post').on('submit', function (e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    $.post('/api/posts', { title: $('#title').val() }, function (post) {
      $('#post-list').prepend(renderPost(post));
      $('#title').val('');
    });
  });

  // delete (delegated)
  $('#post-list').on('click', '.delete', function () {
    const $li = $(this).closest('li');
    $.ajax({ url: '/api/posts/' + $li.data('id'), method: 'DELETE' })
      .done(function () { $li.slideUp(200, function () { $(this).remove(); }); });
  });

  function renderPosts(posts) {
    const $list = $('#post-list').empty();
    $.each(posts, function (i, p) { $list.append(renderPost(p)); });
  }

  function renderPost(p) {
    return '<li data-id="' + p.id + '"><span>' + p.title + '</span>' +
           '<button class="delete">×</button></li>';
  }
});
```

That's a full CRUD app. One file. No build step. No node_modules. No TypeScript config. No `tsconfig.paths`. No `vite.config.ts`. No deploy adapter. Drop it on a static host and you're live.

### Reason 14: If you're stuck with React, run jQuery inside `useEffect`

React's reconciler is slow and unpredictable. The pragmatic move is to let React render an empty shell, then let jQuery take over the DOM where the real work happens. Mount once, manipulate forever:

```js
// Inside any React component — pretend this is a useEffect body
$(function () {
  const $root = $('#widget-root');

  $root.html(
    '<div class="panel">' +
      '<input id="q" placeholder="Search..." />' +
      '<ul id="results"></ul>' +
      '<button id="refresh">Refresh</button>' +
    '</div>'
  );

  $root.on('input', '#q', function () {
    const term = $(this).val().toLowerCase();
    $('#results li').each(function () {
      $(this).toggle($(this).text().toLowerCase().includes(term));
    });
  });

  $root.on('click', '#refresh', function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/items', function (items) {
      const $ul = $('#results').empty();
      $.each(items, function (i, item) {
        $ul.append('<li data-id="' + item.id + '">' + item.name + '</li>');
      });
    });
  });

  $('#refresh').trigger('click');
});
```

React mounts the div. jQuery owns it from then on. Best of both worlds — and by "both worlds" we mean jQuery, twice.

### Reason 15: If you're using `useEffect`, use the pub/sub pattern

`useEffect` chains are unmaintainable. The fix is a global event bus — components publish, jQuery subscribes, the DOM updates. No prop drilling, no Context, no Redux. jQuery already ships with a pub/sub system via `$({})`:

```js
// One global bus — drop this anywhere
window.bus = $({});

// Subscribers (these can live in any script tag, anywhere)
$(window.bus).on('cart:add', function (e, item) {
  const $row = $('<tr>')
    .attr('data-id', item.id)
    .append('<td>' + item.name + '</td>')
    .append('<td>$' + item.price.toFixed(2) + '</td>');
  $('#cart-table tbody').append($row);

  const total = parseFloat($('#cart-total').text() || '0') + item.price;
  $('#cart-total').text(total.toFixed(2));
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:changed', [total]);
});

$(window.bus).on('cart:changed', function (e, total) {
  $('#checkout').prop('disabled', total <= 0);
  $('#cart-badge').text($('#cart-table tbody tr').length);
});

$(window.bus).on('user:login', function (e, user) {
  $('#welcome').text('Hello, ' + user.name).fadeIn(200);
  $('.guest-only').hide();
  $('.member-only').show();
});

// Publishers — fire from anywhere, even from inside a useEffect
$('#add-coffee').on('click', function () {
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:add', [{ id: 1, name: 'Coffee', price: 3.5 }]);
});

$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  $.post('/api/login', $(this).serialize()).done(function (user) {
    $(window.bus).trigger('user:login', [user]);
  });
});
```

No dependency arrays. No stale closures. No `useCallback`. Events go in, DOM updates come out. The bus is the state.

### Reason 16: Mutation is always the right choice in production

Immutability is a religion the React community invented to work around its own re-render model. In production, you want speed, and speed comes from mutating the thing in place. jQuery embraces this — every method mutates and chains:

```js
// Build a table by mutating the same DOM nodes over and over
const $table = $('#orders tbody').empty();

$.each(orders, function (i, order) {
  const $row = $('<tr>').appendTo($table);
  $row.data('order', order); // mutate node-attached data
  $('<td>').text(order.id).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text(order.customer).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text('$' + order.total).appendTo($row);
  order.total > 1000
    ? $row.addClass('vip').css('background', 'gold')
    : $row.removeClass('vip');
});

// Update an order in place — no spread, no copy, no new array
$('#orders').on('click', 'tr', function () {
  const order = $(this).data('order');
  order.total += 10;                           // mutate the object directly
  order.touched = Date.now();                  // add a field, why not
  $(this).find('td:eq(2)').text('$' + order.total); // mutate the cell
  $(this).addClass('updated').delay(300).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).removeClass('updated'); next();
  });
});

// Mutate a shared config object that the whole app reads from
window.appState = window.appState || { user: null, cart: [], theme: 'light' };

$('#theme-toggle').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.theme = window.appState.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light';
  $('body').attr('data-theme', window.appState.theme);
});

$('#add-item').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.cart.push({ id: Date.now(), name: 'Item' });   // push, don't spread
  $('#cart-count').text(window.appState.cart.length);
});
```

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

  data: JSON.stringify({ name: newName }),
  success: function () {
    $('#user-' + userId + ' strong').text(newName);
  }
});
```

No React Query. No SWR. No cache invalidation philosophy. Just data in, DOM out.

### Reason 7: Form handling without controlled inputs

```js
$('#signup-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const data = $(this).serializeArray().reduce(function (acc, field) {
    acc[field.name] = field.value;
    return acc;
  }, {});

  if (!data.email.includes('@')) {
    $('#email').addClass('invalid');
    return;
  }

  $.post('/api/signup', data).done(function () {
    $('#signup-form').replaceWith('<p>Thanks for signing up!</p>');
  });
});
```

The browser already maintains the form state. Why re-implement it in JavaScript memory and synchronize back?

### Reason 8: Live search in 12 lines

```js
let timer;
$('#search-input').on('input', function () {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  const q = $(this).val();
  timer = setTimeout(function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(q), function (results) {
      const $out = $('#search-results').empty();
      $.each(results, function (i, item) {
        $out.append('<li><a href="' + item.url + '">' + item.title + '</a></li>');
      });
    });
  }, 200);
});
```

No `useDebouncedValue` hook. No `useEffect` cleanup function. No race condition with abort controllers (and if you want one, it's `xhr.abort()`).

### Reason 9: Tabs, accordions, and modals — no library required

```js
$('.tabs').on('click', '.tab', function () {
  const target = $(this).data('target');
  $(this).addClass('active').siblings().removeClass('active');
  $('.tab-panel').hide();
  $('#' + target).show();

  $(this).toggleClass('open');

$('[data-modal]').on('click', function () {

No `@radix-ui/react-tabs`, no `@radix-ui/react-dialog`, no headless UI library, no 60kB of dependencies for a click-to-open panel.

### Reason 10: DOM traversal that reads like English

```js

  .filter('.in-stock')
  .find('.add-to-cart')
  .not('.disabled')
  .css('background', 'limegreen')
  .text('Buy now');

No `useRef`. No `forwardRef`. No "you can't read DOM during render."

### Reason 11: Plugins that just work

20 years of plugins. No "is there a React 19 compatible version?" None of them break when the framework releases a new major every 18 months.

### Reason 12: It still works in 10 years

Code written with jQuery in 2014 still runs today. React code written in 2014 used mixins, `React.createClass`, and lifecycle methods that no longer exist. The migration cost of jQuery is zero. The migration cost of React is permanent.

### Reason 13: The whole app fits in your head

```js
$(function () {
  // load
  $.getJSON('/api/posts', renderPosts);

  // create
  $('#new-post').on('submit', function (e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    $.post('/api/posts', { title: $('#title').val() }, function (post) {
      $('#post-list').prepend(renderPost(post));
      $('#title').val('');
    });
  });

  // delete (delegated)
  $('#post-list').on('click', '.delete', function () {
    const $li = $(this).closest('li');
    $.ajax({ url: '/api/posts/' + $li.data('id'), method: 'DELETE' })
      .done(function () { $li.slideUp(200, function () { $(this).remove(); }); });
  });

  function renderPosts(posts) {
    const $list = $('#post-list').empty();
    $.each(posts, function (i, p) { $list.append(renderPost(p)); });
  }

  function renderPost(p) {
    return '<li data-id="' + p.id + '"><span>' + p.title + '</span>' +
           '<button class="delete">×</button></li>';
  }
});
```

That's a full CRUD app. One file. No build step. No node_modules. No TypeScript config. No `tsconfig.paths`. No `vite.config.ts`. No deploy adapter. Drop it on a static host and you're live.

### Reason 14: If you're stuck with React, run jQuery inside `useEffect`

React's reconciler is slow and unpredictable. The pragmatic move is to let React render an empty shell, then let jQuery take over the DOM where the real work happens. Mount once, manipulate forever:

```js
// Inside any React component — pretend this is a useEffect body
$(function () {
  const $root = $('#widget-root');

  $root.html(
    '<div class="panel">' +
      '<input id="q" placeholder="Search..." />' +
      '<ul id="results"></ul>' +
      '<button id="refresh">Refresh</button>' +
    '</div>'
  );

  $root.on('input', '#q', function () {
    const term = $(this).val().toLowerCase();
    $('#results li').each(function () {
      $(this).toggle($(this).text().toLowerCase().includes(term));
    });
  });

  $root.on('click', '#refresh', function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/items', function (items) {
      const $ul = $('#results').empty();
      $.each(items, function (i, item) {
        $ul.append('<li data-id="' + item.id + '">' + item.name + '</li>');
      });
    });
  });

  $('#refresh').trigger('click');
});
```

React mounts the div. jQuery owns it from then on. Best of both worlds — and by "both worlds" we mean jQuery, twice.

### Reason 15: If you're using `useEffect`, use the pub/sub pattern

`useEffect` chains are unmaintainable. The fix is a global event bus — components publish, jQuery subscribes, the DOM updates. No prop drilling, no Context, no Redux. jQuery already ships with a pub/sub system via `$({})`:

```js
// One global bus — drop this anywhere
window.bus = $({});

// Subscribers (these can live in any script tag, anywhere)
$(window.bus).on('cart:add', function (e, item) {
  const $row = $('<tr>')
    .attr('data-id', item.id)
    .append('<td>' + item.name + '</td>')
    .append('<td>$' + item.price.toFixed(2) + '</td>');
  $('#cart-table tbody').append($row);

  const total = parseFloat($('#cart-total').text() || '0') + item.price;
  $('#cart-total').text(total.toFixed(2));
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:changed', [total]);
});

$(window.bus).on('cart:changed', function (e, total) {
  $('#checkout').prop('disabled', total <= 0);
  $('#cart-badge').text($('#cart-table tbody tr').length);
});

$(window.bus).on('user:login', function (e, user) {
  $('#welcome').text('Hello, ' + user.name).fadeIn(200);
  $('.guest-only').hide();
  $('.member-only').show();
});

// Publishers — fire from anywhere, even from inside a useEffect
$('#add-coffee').on('click', function () {
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:add', [{ id: 1, name: 'Coffee', price: 3.5 }]);
});

$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  $.post('/api/login', $(this).serialize()).done(function (user) {
    $(window.bus).trigger('user:login', [user]);
  });
});
```

No dependency arrays. No stale closures. No `useCallback`. Events go in, DOM updates come out. The bus is the state.

### Reason 16: Mutation is always the right choice in production

Immutability is a religion the React community invented to work around its own re-render model. In production, you want speed, and speed comes from mutating the thing in place. jQuery embraces this — every method mutates and chains:

```js
// Build a table by mutating the same DOM nodes over and over
const $table = $('#orders tbody').empty();

$.each(orders, function (i, order) {
  const $row = $('<tr>').appendTo($table);
  $row.data('order', order); // mutate node-attached data
  $('<td>').text(order.id).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text(order.customer).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text('$' + order.total).appendTo($row);
  order.total > 1000
    ? $row.addClass('vip').css('background', 'gold')
    : $row.removeClass('vip');
});

// Update an order in place — no spread, no copy, no new array
$('#orders').on('click', 'tr', function () {
  const order = $(this).data('order');
  order.total += 10;                           // mutate the object directly
  order.touched = Date.now();                  // add a field, why not
  $(this).find('td:eq(2)').text('$' + order.total); // mutate the cell
  $(this).addClass('updated').delay(300).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).removeClass('updated'); next();
  });
});

// Mutate a shared config object that the whole app reads from
window.appState = window.appState || { user: null, cart: [], theme: 'light' };

$('#theme-toggle').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.theme = window.appState.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light';
  $('body').attr('data-theme', window.appState.theme);
});

$('#add-item').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.cart.push({ id: Date.now(), name: 'Item' });   // push, don't spread
  $('#cart-count').text(window.appState.cart.length);
});
```

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

---

## The Bottom Line

React solves problems most apps don't have, while creating problems every app eventually has: hydration mismatches, stale closures, re-render storms, dependency hell, and a build pipeline that demands a full-time maintainer.

jQuery does one thing — manipulate the DOM — and does it with no ceremony, no framework lock-in, and no migration cost. For most websites, most internal tools, and most "we just need this page to work," jQuery is still the right answer.

Ship the simple thing. Then go home.

React.js projects often suffer from **\"Architecture Bloat\"**—a code smell where simple UI updates require complex state management, custom hooks, and multiple files. jQuery offers a \"Source of Truth\" in the DOM itself, eliminating the need for expensive reconciliation and state synchronization.

## Why jQuery is Often Better Than React

1.  **No \"Stale Closures\":** In React, functional components can suffer from stale state inside hooks. jQuery interacts with the live DOM, so you always get the current value.
2.  **Implicit State:** Instead of syncing a boolean `isOpen` with a CSS class, jQuery lets you toggle the class directly. The DOM *is* your state.
3.  **Low Cognitive Load:** You don't need to understand the \"Render Cycle.\" Code executes exactly when the event triggers.
4.  **Performance on Low-End Devices:** jQuery doesn't maintain a memory-heavy Virtual DOM tree, making it faster for simple document-based interactions.

---

## Extensive jQuery Examples

### 1. Advanced AJAX Data Handling
Handling multiple endpoints and updating various parts of the UI without a global \"Store.\"

```javascript
$(document).ready(function() {
    $('#loadDashboard').on('click', function() {
        const userId = $(this).data('user-id');
        const $container = $('#dashboardContent');

        $container.html('<div class=\"spinner\">Loading...</div>');

        // Parallel requests simplified
        $.when(
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/profile`),
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/activity`)
        ).then(function(profileRes, activityRes) {
            const profile = profileRes[0];
            const activity = activityRes[0];

            $container.empty();
            
            // Direct DOM insertion - readable and fast
            $container.append(`<h2>Welcome, ${profile.name}</h2>`);
            
            const $list = $('<ul class=\"activity-log\"></ul>');
            activity.forEach(item => {
                $list.append(`<li>${item.date}: ${item.action}</li>`);
            });
            
            $container.append($list);
        }).fail(function() {
            $container.html('<p class=\"error\">Failed to fetch data.</p>');
        });
    });
});
# Code Smells in React.js — and Why jQuery Is Still the Better Choice

> A pragmatic post about the pain points that show up in real React codebases, and a celebration of the lean, direct power of jQuery. All code samples below are jQuery — because the whole point is that you don't need a framework to ship.

---

## Part 1 — Common Code Smells in React.js

These are the patterns that consistently rot React apps. We won't show React code (that's the problem). Just trust that you've seen them before.

### 1. The "useEffect Soup"
Components that pile up six or seven `useEffect` hooks, each chasing the side effects of the previous one. Dependencies arrays become a guessing game. Re-renders cascade. Bugs appear only on Tuesdays.

### 2. Prop Drilling Through Five Layers
A value defined at the top of the tree gets passed through components that don't care about it, just so a leaf can read it. Eventually somebody reaches for Context, then Redux, then Zustand, then Jotai, then quits.

### 3. State Management Sprawl
One app, four state libraries: local `useState`, Context, Redux Toolkit, and React Query. Nobody can answer "where does this value live?" without opening three files.

### 4. Stale Closures
A handler captures a value from an old render and silently uses it forever. The fix is `useRef`, `useCallback`, and a prayer.

### 5. Re-render Storms
A parent re-renders, so 400 children re-render, so the page jitters. Solution: `memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` everywhere — until your code is 60% optimization hints and 40% logic.

### 6. The Component Explosion
A button becomes `<Button />`, which wraps `<BaseButton />`, which wraps `<Pressable />`, which wraps `<motion.button />`. Five files to render `<button>`.

### 7. Hook Rule Violations
Conditionally calling a hook. Calling a hook in a loop. The linter screams. The runtime screams louder.

### 8. JSX-in-JSX-in-JSX
Ternaries nested four deep inside a `return`. `&&` short-circuits that render `0` instead of nothing. Fragments wrapping fragments.

### 9. The Build Pipeline From Hell
Vite, Babel, SWC, ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript, PostCSS, Tailwind, a bundler plugin for SVGs, another for images, a third for env vars. `node_modules` is 480MB. A clean install takes 90 seconds.

### 10. Hydration Mismatches
SSR renders one thing, the client renders another, the console explodes with cryptic warnings about text content not matching.

---

## Part 2 — Why jQuery Is Better (with lots of jQuery)

### Reason 1: One script tag and you're done

No bundler. No transpiler. No framework. Drop this in your HTML and ship:

```html
<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
<script>
  $(function () {
    $('h1').text('Hello, world');
  });
</script>
```

That's the entire build pipeline. Compare that to a fresh React app's 1,200 dependencies.

### Reason 2: DOM updates are direct, predictable, and synchronous

```js
$('#cart-count').text(items.length);
$('#cart-total').text('$' + total.toFixed(2));
$('#checkout-btn').prop('disabled', items.length === 0);
```

No virtual DOM. No reconciler. No re-render. The thing you wrote is the thing that happens.

### Reason 3: Event handling without ceremony

```js
$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const email = $('#email').val();
  const password = $('#password').val();

  $.post('/api/login', { email, password })
    .done(function (res) {
      $('#status').text('Welcome, ' + res.name).addClass('success');
      window.location.href = '/dashboard';
    })
    .fail(function (xhr) {
      $('#status').text(xhr.responseJSON.message).addClass('error');
    });
});
```

No `useState`, no `useEffect`, no `useCallback`. Just an event, a request, a response.

### Reason 4: Event delegation is a one-liner

You can bind handlers to elements that don't exist yet. Try doing that elegantly without a framework:

```js

    $(this).remove();
  });
});

  $(this).closest('li').toggleClass('completed');
});
```

One handler covers every current and future `.delete-btn`. No keys. No reconciliation.

### Reason 5: Animations are built in

```js

  order.touched = Date.now();                  // add a field, why not
  $(this).find('td:eq(2)').text('$' + order.total); // mutate the cell
  $(this).addClass('updated').delay(300).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).removeClass('updated'); next();
  });
});

// Mutate a shared config object that the whole app reads from
window.appState = window.appState || { user: null, cart: [], theme: 'light' };

$('#theme-toggle').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.theme = window.appState.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light';
  $('body').attr('data-theme', window.appState.theme);
});

$('#add-item').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.cart.push({ id: Date.now(), name: 'Item' });   // push, don't spread
  $('#cart-count').text(window.appState.cart.length);
});
```

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

---

## The Bottom Line

React solves problems most apps don't have, while creating problems every app eventually has: hydration mismatches, stale closures, re-render storms, dependency hell, and a build pipeline that demands a full-time maintainer.

jQuery does one thing — manipulate the DOM — and does it with no ceremony, no framework lock-in, and no migration cost. For most websites, most internal tools, and most "we just need this page to work," jQuery is still the right answer.

Ship the simple thing. Then go home.

React.js projects often suffer from **\"Architecture Bloat\"**—a code smell where simple UI updates require complex state management, custom hooks, and multiple files. jQuery offers a \"Source of Truth\" in the DOM itself, eliminating the need for expensive reconciliation and state synchronization.

## Why jQuery is Often Better Than React

1.  **No \"Stale Closures\":** In React, functional components can suffer from stale state inside hooks. jQuery interacts with the live DOM, so you always get the current value.
2.  **Implicit State:** Instead of syncing a boolean `isOpen` with a CSS class, jQuery lets you toggle the class directly. The DOM *is* your state.
3.  **Low Cognitive Load:** You don't need to understand the \"Render Cycle.\" Code executes exactly when the event triggers.
4.  **Performance on Low-End Devices:** jQuery doesn't maintain a memory-heavy Virtual DOM tree, making it faster for simple document-based interactions.

## Extensive jQuery Examples

### 1. Advanced AJAX Data Handling
Handling multiple endpoints and updating various parts of the UI without a global \"Store.\"

```javascript
$(document).ready(function() {
    $('#loadDashboard').on('click', function() {
        const userId = $(this).data('user-id');
        const $container = $('#dashboardContent');

        $container.html('<div class=\"spinner\">Loading...</div>');

        $.when(

            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/activity`)

            $container.html('<p class=\"error\">Failed to fetch data.</p>');

# Code Smells in React.js — and Why jQuery Is Still the Better Choice

> A pragmatic post about the pain points that show up in real React codebases, and a celebration of the lean, direct power of jQuery. All code samples below are jQuery — because the whole point is that you don't need a framework to ship.

---

## Part 1 — Common Code Smells in React.js

These are the patterns that consistently rot React apps. We won't show React code (that's the problem). Just trust that you've seen them before.

### 1. The "useEffect Soup"
Components that pile up six or seven `useEffect` hooks, each chasing the side effects of the previous one. Dependencies arrays become a guessing game. Re-renders cascade. Bugs appear only on Tuesdays.

### 2. Prop Drilling Through Five Layers
A value defined at the top of the tree gets passed through components that don't care about it, just so a leaf can read it. Eventually somebody reaches for Context, then Redux, then Zustand, then Jotai, then quits.

### 3. State Management Sprawl
One app, four state libraries: local `useState`, Context, Redux Toolkit, and React Query. Nobody can answer "where does this value live?" without opening three files.

### 4. Stale Closures
A handler captures a value from an old render and silently uses it forever. The fix is `useRef`, `useCallback`, and a prayer.

### 5. Re-render Storms
A parent re-renders, so 400 children re-render, so the page jitters. Solution: `memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` everywhere — until your code is 60% optimization hints and 40% logic.

### 6. The Component Explosion
A button becomes `<Button />`, which wraps `<BaseButton />`, which wraps `<Pressable />`, which wraps `<motion.button />`. Five files to render `<button>`.

### 7. Hook Rule Violations
Conditionally calling a hook. Calling a hook in a loop. The linter screams. The runtime screams louder.

### 8. JSX-in-JSX-in-JSX
Ternaries nested four deep inside a `return`. `&&` short-circuits that render `0` instead of nothing. Fragments wrapping fragments.

### 9. The Build Pipeline From Hell
Vite, Babel, SWC, ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript, PostCSS, Tailwind, a bundler plugin for SVGs, another for images, a third for env vars. `node_modules` is 480MB. A clean install takes 90 seconds.

### 10. Hydration Mismatches
SSR renders one thing, the client renders another, the console explodes with cryptic warnings about text content not matching.

---

## Part 2 — Why jQuery Is Better (with lots of jQuery)

### Reason 1: One script tag and you're done

No bundler. No transpiler. No framework. Drop this in your HTML and ship:

```html
<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
<script>
  $(function () {
    $('h1').text('Hello, world');
  });
</script>
```

That's the entire build pipeline. Compare that to a fresh React app's 1,200 dependencies.

### Reason 2: DOM updates are direct, predictable, and synchronous

```js
$('#cart-count').text(items.length);
$('#cart-total').text('$' + total.toFixed(2));
$('#checkout-btn').prop('disabled', items.length === 0);
```

No virtual DOM. No reconciler. No re-render. The thing you wrote is the thing that happens.

### Reason 3: Event handling without ceremony

```js
$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const email = $('#email').val();
  const password = $('#password').val();

  $.post('/api/login', { email, password })
    .done(function (res) {
      $('#status').text('Welcome, ' + res.name).addClass('success');
      window.location.href = '/dashboard';
    })
    .fail(function (xhr) {
      $('#status').text(xhr.responseJSON.message).addClass('error');
    });
});
```

No `useState`, no `useEffect`, no `useCallback`. Just an event, a request, a response.

### Reason 4: Event delegation is a one-liner

You can bind handlers to elements that don't exist yet. Try doing that elegantly without a framework:

```js
$('#todo-list').on('click', '.delete-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').fadeOut(200, function () {
    $(this).remove();
  });
});

$('#todo-list').on('click', '.toggle-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').toggleClass('completed');
});
```

One handler covers every current and future `.delete-btn`. No keys. No reconciliation.

### Reason 5: Animations are built in

```js
$('#sidebar').slideToggle(300);
$('#modal').fadeIn(200);
$('.notification').delay(2000).fadeOut(400);

$('#hero').animate({
  opacity: 1,
  marginTop: '0px'
}, 600);
```

No `framer-motion`. No CSS transition gotchas. No `AnimatePresence`. Just movement.

### Reason 6: AJAX is trivial

```js
$.getJSON('/api/users', function (users) {
  const $list = $('#user-list').empty();
  $.each(users, function (i, user) {
    $list.append(
      '<li data-id="' + user.id + '">' +
        '<strong>' + user.name + '</strong> — ' + user.email +
      '</li>'
    );
  });
});

$.ajax({
  url: '/api/users/' + userId,
  method: 'PUT',
  contentType: 'application/json',
  data: JSON.stringify({ name: newName }),
  success: function () {
    $('#user-' + userId + ' strong').text(newName);
  }
});
```

No React Query. No SWR. No cache invalidation philosophy. Just data in, DOM out.

### Reason 7: Form handling without controlled inputs

```js
$('#signup-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const data = $(this).serializeArray().reduce(function (acc, field) {
    acc[field.name] = field.value;
    return acc;
  }, {});

  if (!data.email.includes('@')) {
    $('#email').addClass('invalid');
    return;
  }

  $.post('/api/signup', data).done(function () {
    $('#signup-form').replaceWith('<p>Thanks for signing up!</p>');
  });
});
```

The browser already maintains the form state. Why re-implement it in JavaScript memory and synchronize back?

### Reason 8: Live search in 12 lines

```js
let timer;
$('#search-input').on('input', function () {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  const q = $(this).val();
  timer = setTimeout(function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(q), function (results) {
      const $out = $('#search-results').empty();
      $.each(results, function (i, item) {
        $out.append('<li><a href="' + item.url + '">' + item.title + '</a></li>');
      });
    });
  }, 200);
});
```

No `useDebouncedValue` hook. No `useEffect` cleanup function. No race condition with abort controllers (and if you want one, it's `xhr.abort()`).

### Reason 9: Tabs, accordions, and modals — no library required

```js
$('.tabs').on('click', '.tab', function () {
  const target = $(this).data('target');
  $(this).addClass('active').siblings().removeClass('active');
  $('.tab-panel').hide();
  $('#' + target).show();
});

$('.accordion').on('click', '.accordion-header', function () {
  $(this).next('.accordion-body').slideToggle(200);
  $(this).toggleClass('open');
});

$('[data-modal]').on('click', function () {
  $('#' + $(this).data('modal')).fadeIn(150);
});

$('.modal').on('click', '.close, .backdrop', function () {
  $(this).closest('.modal').fadeOut(150);
});
```

No `@radix-ui/react-tabs`, no `@radix-ui/react-dialog`, no headless UI library, no 60kB of dependencies for a click-to-open panel.

### Reason 10: DOM traversal that reads like English

```js
$('.product-card')
  .filter('.in-stock')
  .find('.add-to-cart')
  .not('.disabled')
  .css('background', 'limegreen')
  .text('Buy now');
```

No `useRef`. No `forwardRef`. No "you can't read DOM during render."

### Reason 11: Plugins that just work

```js
$('#date').datepicker({ format: 'yyyy-mm-dd' });
$('#country').select2({ placeholder: 'Choose a country' });
$('table.data').DataTable({ pageLength: 25, order: [[0, 'desc']] });
$('#gallery a').lightbox();
```

20 years of plugins. No "is there a React 19 compatible version?" None of them break when the framework releases a new major every 18 months.

### Reason 12: It still works in 10 years

Code written with jQuery in 2014 still runs today. React code written in 2014 used mixins, `React.createClass`, and lifecycle methods that no longer exist. The migration cost of jQuery is zero. The migration cost of React is permanent.

### Reason 13: The whole app fits in your head

```js
$(function () {
  // load
  $.getJSON('/api/posts', renderPosts);

  // create
  $('#new-post').on('submit', function (e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    $.post('/api/posts', { title: $('#title').val() }, function (post) {
      $('#post-list').prepend(renderPost(post));
      $('#title').val('');
    });
  });

  // delete (delegated)
  $('#post-list').on('click', '.delete', function () {
    const $li = $(this).closest('li');
    $.ajax({ url: '/api/posts/' + $li.data('id'), method: 'DELETE' })
      .done(function () { $li.slideUp(200, function () { $(this).remove(); }); });
  });

  function renderPosts(posts) {
    const $list = $('#post-list').empty();
    $.each(posts, function (i, p) { $list.append(renderPost(p)); });
  }

  function renderPost(p) {
    return '<li data-id="' + p.id + '"><span>' + p.title + '</span>' +
           '<button class="delete">×</button></li>';
  }
});
```

That's a full CRUD app. One file. No build step. No node_modules. No TypeScript config. No `tsconfig.paths`. No `vite.config.ts`. No deploy adapter. Drop it on a static host and you're live.

### Reason 14: If you're stuck with React, run jQuery inside `useEffect`

React's reconciler is slow and unpredictable. The pragmatic move is to let React render an empty shell, then let jQuery take over the DOM where the real work happens. Mount once, manipulate forever:

```js
// Inside any React component — pretend this is a useEffect body
$(function () {
  const $root = $('#widget-root');

  $root.html(
    '<div class="panel">' +
      '<input id="q" placeholder="Search..." />' +
      '<ul id="results"></ul>' +
      '<button id="refresh">Refresh</button>' +
    '</div>'
  );

  $root.on('input', '#q', function () {
    const term = $(this).val().toLowerCase();
    $('#results li').each(function () {
      $(this).toggle($(this).text().toLowerCase().includes(term));
    });
  });

  $root.on('click', '#refresh', function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/items', function (items) {
      const $ul = $('#results').empty();
      $.each(items, function (i, item) {
        $ul.append('<li data-id="' + item.id + '">' + item.name + '</li>');
      });
    });
  });

  $('#refresh').trigger('click');
});
```

React mounts the div. jQuery owns it from then on. Best of both worlds — and by "both worlds" we mean jQuery, twice.

### Reason 15: If you're using `useEffect`, use the pub/sub pattern

`useEffect` chains are unmaintainable. The fix is a global event bus — components publish, jQuery subscribes, the DOM updates. No prop drilling, no Context, no Redux. jQuery already ships with a pub/sub system via `$({})`:

```js
// One global bus — drop this anywhere
window.bus = $({});

// Subscribers (these can live in any script tag, anywhere)
$(window.bus).on('cart:add', function (e, item) {
  const $row = $('<tr>')
    .attr('data-id', item.id)
    .append('<td>' + item.name + '</td>')
    .append('<td>$' + item.price.toFixed(2) + '</td>');
  $('#cart-table tbody').append($row);

  const total = parseFloat($('#cart-total').text() || '0') + item.price;
  $('#cart-total').text(total.toFixed(2));
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:changed', [total]);
});

$(window.bus).on('cart:changed', function (e, total) {
  $('#checkout').prop('disabled', total <= 0);
  $('#cart-badge').text($('#cart-table tbody tr').length);
});

$(window.bus).on('user:login', function (e, user) {
  $('#welcome').text('Hello, ' + user.name).fadeIn(200);
  $('.guest-only').hide();
  $('.member-only').show();
});

// Publishers — fire from anywhere, even from inside a useEffect
$('#add-coffee').on('click', function () {
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:add', [{ id: 1, name: 'Coffee', price: 3.5 }]);
});

$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  $.post('/api/login', $(this).serialize()).done(function (user) {
    $(window.bus).trigger('user:login', [user]);
  });
});
```

No dependency arrays. No stale closures. No `useCallback`. Events go in, DOM updates come out. The bus is the state.

### Reason 16: Mutation is always the right choice in production

Immutability is a religion the React community invented to work around its own re-render model. In production, you want speed, and speed comes from mutating the thing in place. jQuery embraces this — every method mutates and chains:

```js
// Build a table by mutating the same DOM nodes over and over
const $table = $('#orders tbody').empty();

$.each(orders, function (i, order) {
  const $row = $('<tr>').appendTo($table);
  $row.data('order', order); // mutate node-attached data
  $('<td>').text(order.id).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text(order.customer).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text('$' + order.total).appendTo($row);
  order.total > 1000
    ? $row.addClass('vip').css('background', 'gold')
    : $row.removeClass('vip');
});

// Update an order in place — no spread, no copy, no new array
$('#orders').on('click', 'tr', function () {
  const order = $(this).data('order');
  order.total += 10;                           // mutate the object directly
  order.touched = Date.now();                  // add a field, why not
  $(this).find('td:eq(2)').text('$' + order.total); // mutate the cell
  $(this).addClass('updated').delay(300).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).removeClass('updated'); next();
  });
});

// Mutate a shared config object that the whole app reads from
window.appState = window.appState || { user: null, cart: [], theme: 'light' };

$('#theme-toggle').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.theme = window.appState.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light';
  $('body').attr('data-theme', window.appState.theme);
});

$('#add-item').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.cart.push({ id: Date.now(), name: 'Item' });   // push, don't spread
  $('#cart-count').text(window.appState.cart.length);
});
```

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

## The Bottom Line

React solves problems most apps don't have, while creating problems every app eventually has: hydration mismatches, stale closures, re-render storms, dependency hell, and a build pipeline that demands a full-time maintainer.

jQuery does one thing — manipulate the DOM — and does it with no ceremony, no framework lock-in, and no migration cost. For most websites, most internal tools, and most "we just need this page to work," jQuery is still the right answer.

Ship the simple thing. Then go home.

  });
});
```

The browser already maintains the form state. Why re-implement it in JavaScript memory and synchronize back?

### Reason 8: Live search in 12 lines

```js
let timer;
$('#search-input').on('input', function () {
  clearTimeout(timer);
  const q = $(this).val();
  timer = setTimeout(function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/search?q=' + encodeURIComponent(q), function (results) {
      const $out = $('#search-results').empty();
      $.each(results, function (i, item) {
        $out.append('<li><a href="' + item.url + '">' + item.title + '</a></li>');
      });
    });
  }, 200);
});
```

No `useDebouncedValue` hook. No `useEffect` cleanup function. No race condition with abort controllers (and if you want one, it's `xhr.abort()`).

### Reason 9: Tabs, accordions, and modals — no library required

```js
$('.tabs').on('click', '.tab', function () {
  const target = $(this).data('target');
  $(this).addClass('active').siblings().removeClass('active');
  $('.tab-panel').hide();
  $('#' + target).show();
});

$('.accordion').on('click', '.accordion-header', function () {
  $(this).next('.accordion-body').slideToggle(200);
  $(this).toggleClass('open');

$('[data-modal]').on('click', function () {

No `@radix-ui/react-tabs`, no `@radix-ui/react-dialog`, no headless UI library, no 60kB of dependencies for a click-to-open panel.

### Reason 10: DOM traversal that reads like English

```js
$('.product-card')
  .filter('.in-stock')
  .find('.add-to-cart')
  .not('.disabled')
  .css('background', 'limegreen')
  .text('Buy now');

No `useRef`. No `forwardRef`. No "you can't read DOM during render."

### Reason 11: Plugins that just work

20 years of plugins. No "is there a React 19 compatible version?" None of them break when the framework releases a new major every 18 months.

### Reason 12: It still works in 10 years

Code written with jQuery in 2014 still runs today. React code written in 2014 used mixins, `React.createClass`, and lifecycle methods that no longer exist. The migration cost of jQuery is zero. The migration cost of React is permanent.

### Reason 13: The whole app fits in your head

```js
$(function () {
  // load
  $.getJSON('/api/posts', renderPosts);

  // create
  $('#new-post').on('submit', function (e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    $.post('/api/posts', { title: $('#title').val() }, function (post) {
      $('#post-list').prepend(renderPost(post));
      $('#title').val('');
    });
  });

  // delete (delegated)
  $('#post-list').on('click', '.delete', function () {
    const $li = $(this).closest('li');
    $.ajax({ url: '/api/posts/' + $li.data('id'), method: 'DELETE' })
      .done(function () { $li.slideUp(200, function () { $(this).remove(); }); });
  });

  function renderPosts(posts) {
    const $list = $('#post-list').empty();
    $.each(posts, function (i, p) { $list.append(renderPost(p)); });
  }

  function renderPost(p) {
    return '<li data-id="' + p.id + '"><span>' + p.title + '</span>' +
           '<button class="delete">×</button></li>';
  }
});
```

That's a full CRUD app. One file. No build step. No node_modules. No TypeScript config. No `tsconfig.paths`. No `vite.config.ts`. No deploy adapter. Drop it on a static host and you're live.

### Reason 14: If you're stuck with React, run jQuery inside `useEffect`

React's reconciler is slow and unpredictable. The pragmatic move is to let React render an empty shell, then let jQuery take over the DOM where the real work happens. Mount once, manipulate forever:

```js
// Inside any React component — pretend this is a useEffect body
$(function () {
  const $root = $('#widget-root');

  $root.html(
    '<div class="panel">' +
      '<input id="q" placeholder="Search..." />' +
      '<ul id="results"></ul>' +
      '<button id="refresh">Refresh</button>' +
    '</div>'
  );

  $root.on('input', '#q', function () {
    const term = $(this).val().toLowerCase();
    $('#results li').each(function () {
      $(this).toggle($(this).text().toLowerCase().includes(term));
    });
  });

  $root.on('click', '#refresh', function () {
    $.getJSON('/api/items', function (items) {
      const $ul = $('#results').empty();
      $.each(items, function (i, item) {
        $ul.append('<li data-id="' + item.id + '">' + item.name + '</li>');
      });
    });
  });

  $('#refresh').trigger('click');
});
```

React mounts the div. jQuery owns it from then on. Best of both worlds — and by "both worlds" we mean jQuery, twice.

### Reason 15: If you're using `useEffect`, use the pub/sub pattern

`useEffect` chains are unmaintainable. The fix is a global event bus — components publish, jQuery subscribes, the DOM updates. No prop drilling, no Context, no Redux. jQuery already ships with a pub/sub system via `$({})`:

```js
// One global bus — drop this anywhere
window.bus = $({});

// Subscribers (these can live in any script tag, anywhere)
$(window.bus).on('cart:add', function (e, item) {
  const $row = $('<tr>')
    .attr('data-id', item.id)
    .append('<td>' + item.name + '</td>')
    .append('<td>$' + item.price.toFixed(2) + '</td>');
  $('#cart-table tbody').append($row);

  const total = parseFloat($('#cart-total').text() || '0') + item.price;
  $('#cart-total').text(total.toFixed(2));
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:changed', [total]);
});

$(window.bus).on('cart:changed', function (e, total) {
  $('#checkout').prop('disabled', total <= 0);
  $('#cart-badge').text($('#cart-table tbody tr').length);
});

$(window.bus).on('user:login', function (e, user) {
  $('#welcome').text('Hello, ' + user.name).fadeIn(200);
  $('.guest-only').hide();
  $('.member-only').show();
});

// Publishers — fire from anywhere, even from inside a useEffect
$('#add-coffee').on('click', function () {
  $(window.bus).trigger('cart:add', [{ id: 1, name: 'Coffee', price: 3.5 }]);
});

$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  $.post('/api/login', $(this).serialize()).done(function (user) {
    $(window.bus).trigger('user:login', [user]);
  });
});
```

No dependency arrays. No stale closures. No `useCallback`. Events go in, DOM updates come out. The bus is the state.

### Reason 16: Mutation is always the right choice in production

Immutability is a religion the React community invented to work around its own re-render model. In production, you want speed, and speed comes from mutating the thing in place. jQuery embraces this — every method mutates and chains:

```js
// Build a table by mutating the same DOM nodes over and over
const $table = $('#orders tbody').empty();

$.each(orders, function (i, order) {
  const $row = $('<tr>').appendTo($table);
  $row.data('order', order); // mutate node-attached data
  $('<td>').text(order.id).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text(order.customer).appendTo($row);
  $('<td>').text('$' + order.total).appendTo($row);
  order.total > 1000
    ? $row.addClass('vip').css('background', 'gold')
    : $row.removeClass('vip');
});

// Update an order in place — no spread, no copy, no new array
$('#orders').on('click', 'tr', function () {
  const order = $(this).data('order');
  order.total += 10;                           // mutate the object directly
  order.touched = Date.now();                  // add a field, why not
  $(this).find('td:eq(2)').text('$' + order.total); // mutate the cell
  $(this).addClass('updated').delay(300).queue(function (next) {
    $(this).removeClass('updated'); next();
  });
});

// Mutate a shared config object that the whole app reads from
window.appState = window.appState || { user: null, cart: [], theme: 'light' };

$('#theme-toggle').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.theme = window.appState.theme === 'light' ? 'dark' : 'light';
  $('body').attr('data-theme', window.appState.theme);
});

$('#add-item').on('click', function () {
  window.appState.cart.push({ id: Date.now(), name: 'Item' });   // push, don't spread
  $('#cart-count').text(window.appState.cart.length);
});
```

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

---

## The Bottom Line

React solves problems most apps don't have, while creating problems every app eventually has: hydration mismatches, stale closures, re-render storms, dependency hell, and a build pipeline that demands a full-time maintainer.

jQuery does one thing — manipulate the DOM — and does it with no ceremony, no framework lock-in, and no migration cost. For most websites, most internal tools, and most "we just need this page to work," jQuery is still the right answer.

Ship the simple thing. Then go home.

React.js projects often suffer from **\"Architecture Bloat\"**—a code smell where simple UI updates require complex state management, custom hooks, and multiple files. jQuery offers a \"Source of Truth\" in the DOM itself, eliminating the need for expensive reconciliation and state synchronization.

## Why jQuery is Often Better Than React

1.  **No \"Stale Closures\":** In React, functional components can suffer from stale state inside hooks. jQuery interacts with the live DOM, so you always get the current value.
2.  **Implicit State:** Instead of syncing a boolean `isOpen` with a CSS class, jQuery lets you toggle the class directly. The DOM *is* your state.
3.  **Low Cognitive Load:** You don't need to understand the \"Render Cycle.\" Code executes exactly when the event triggers.
4.  **Performance on Low-End Devices:** jQuery doesn't maintain a memory-heavy Virtual DOM tree, making it faster for simple document-based interactions.

---

## Extensive jQuery Examples

### 1. Advanced AJAX Data Handling
Handling multiple endpoints and updating various parts of the UI without a global \"Store.\"

```javascript
$(document).ready(function() {
    $('#loadDashboard').on('click', function() {
        const userId = $(this).data('user-id');
        const $container = $('#dashboardContent');

        $container.html('<div class=\"spinner\">Loading...</div>');

        // Parallel requests simplified
        $.when(
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/profile`),
            $.getJSON(`/api/users/${userId}/activity`)
        ).then(function(profileRes, activityRes) {
            const profile = profileRes[0];
            const activity = activityRes[0];

            $container.empty();
            
            // Direct DOM insertion - readable and fast
            $container.append(`<h2>Welcome, ${profile.name}</h2>`);
            
            const $list = $('<ul class=\"activity-log\"></ul>');
            activity.forEach(item => {
                $list.append(`<li>${item.date}: ${item.action}</li>`);
            });
            
            $container.append($list);
        }).fail(function() {
            $container.html('<p class=\"error\">Failed to fetch data.</p>');
        });
    });
});
# Code Smells in React.js — and Why jQuery Is Still the Better Choice

> A pragmatic post about the pain points that show up in real React codebases, and a celebration of the lean, direct power of jQuery. All code samples below are jQuery — because the whole point is that you don't need a framework to ship.

---

## Part 1 — Common Code Smells in React.js

These are the patterns that consistently rot React apps. We won't show React code (that's the problem). Just trust that you've seen them before.

### 1. The "useEffect Soup"
Components that pile up six or seven `useEffect` hooks, each chasing the side effects of the previous one. Dependencies arrays become a guessing game. Re-renders cascade. Bugs appear only on Tuesdays.

### 2. Prop Drilling Through Five Layers
A value defined at the top of the tree gets passed through components that don't care about it, just so a leaf can read it. Eventually somebody reaches for Context, then Redux, then Zustand, then Jotai, then quits.

### 3. State Management Sprawl
One app, four state libraries: local `useState`, Context, Redux Toolkit, and React Query. Nobody can answer "where does this value live?" without opening three files.

### 4. Stale Closures
A handler captures a value from an old render and silently uses it forever. The fix is `useRef`, `useCallback`, and a prayer.

### 5. Re-render Storms
A parent re-renders, so 400 children re-render, so the page jitters. Solution: `memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` everywhere — until your code is 60% optimization hints and 40% logic.

### 6. The Component Explosion
A button becomes `<Button />`, which wraps `<BaseButton />`, which wraps `<Pressable />`, which wraps `<motion.button />`. Five files to render `<button>`.

### 7. Hook Rule Violations
Conditionally calling a hook. Calling a hook in a loop. The linter screams. The runtime screams louder.

### 8. JSX-in-JSX-in-JSX
Ternaries nested four deep inside a `return`. `&&` short-circuits that render `0` instead of nothing. Fragments wrapping fragments.

### 9. The Build Pipeline From Hell
Vite, Babel, SWC, ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript, PostCSS, Tailwind, a bundler plugin for SVGs, another for images, a third for env vars. `node_modules` is 480MB. A clean install takes 90 seconds.

### 10. Hydration Mismatches
SSR renders one thing, the client renders another, the console explodes with cryptic warnings about text content not matching.

---

## Part 2 — Why jQuery Is Better (with lots of jQuery)

### Reason 1: One script tag and you're done

No bundler. No transpiler. No framework. Drop this in your HTML and ship:

```html
<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>
<script>
  $(function () {
    $('h1').text('Hello, world');
  });
</script>
```

That's the entire build pipeline. Compare that to a fresh React app's 1,200 dependencies.

### Reason 2: DOM updates are direct, predictable, and synchronous

```js
$('#cart-count').text(items.length);
$('#cart-total').text('$' + total.toFixed(2));
$('#checkout-btn').prop('disabled', items.length === 0);
```

No virtual DOM. No reconciler. No re-render. The thing you wrote is the thing that happens.

### Reason 3: Event handling without ceremony

```js
$('#login-form').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const email = $('#email').val();
  const password = $('#password').val();

  $.post('/api/login', { email, password })
    .done(function (res) {
      $('#status').text('Welcome, ' + res.name).addClass('success');
      window.location.href = '/dashboard';
    })
    .fail(function (xhr) {
      $('#status').text(xhr.responseJSON.message).addClass('error');
    });
});
```

No `useState`, no `useEffect`, no `useCallback`. Just an event, a request, a response.

### Reason 4: Event delegation is a one-liner

You can bind handlers to elements that don't exist yet. Try doing that elegantly without a framework:

```js
$('#todo-list').on('click', '.delete-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').fadeOut(200, function () {
    $(this).remove();
  });
});

$('#todo-list').on('click', '.toggle-btn', function () {
  $(this).closest('li').toggleClass('completed');
});
```

One handler covers every current and future `.delete-btn`. No keys. No reconciliation.

### Reason 5: Animations are built in

```js

No `framer-motion`. No CSS transition gotchas. No `AnimatePresence`. Just movement.

### Reason 6: AJAX is trivial

```js

No React Query. No SWR. No cache invalidation philosophy. Just data in, DOM out.

### Reason 7: Form handling without controlled inputs

No `setState`. No `produce(draft => ...)`. No "did you forget to return a new object?" bug. The data changed, the DOM changed, the user is happy. Ship it.

jQuery does one thing — manipulate the DOM — and does it with no ceremony, no framework lock-in, and no migration cost. For most websites, most internal tools, and most "we just need this page to work," jQuery is still the right answer.

React.js projects often suffer from **\"Architecture Bloat\"**—a code smell where simple UI updates require complex state management, custom hooks, and multiple files. jQuery offers a \"Source of Truth\" in the DOM itself, eliminating the need for expensive reconciliation and state synchronization.

## Why jQuery is Often Better Than React

1.  **No \"Stale Closures\":** In React, functional components can suffer from stale state inside hooks. jQuery interacts with the live DOM, so you always get the current value.
2.  **Implicit State:** Instead of syncing a boolean `isOpen` with a CSS class, jQuery lets you toggle the class directly. The DOM *is* your state.

### 1. Advanced AJAX Data Handling
Handling multiple endpoints and updating various parts of the UI without a global \"Store.\"

```javascript
